title: Alabama Tornado Disaster
description: On April 27, 2011, the state of Alabama was devastated by a collection of tornadoes that rendered the city powerless for days. Army Materiel Command (AMC) civil service employee Suzanne Tillery took us through the destruction of her home. Also available in high definition.
keywords: tornado, Army Materiel Command, AMC Civilian Employees, Suzanne Tillery, High Definition, Alabama, disaster

transcript.text: Hi, I'm Cherish Washington from AMC Public Affairs and we're interrupting our regular news dispatch to talk about preparation in the event of a tornado.
On April 27th, a storm of historic proportions ripped through Northern Alabama
and today I'm here with Sue Taylor from the Office of Public and Congressional Affairs
and she's going to take us through what was her Athens home.
Well, this is what is left of my home after our F5 tornado hit it on April 27th.
Without the weather radio, I probably would have just ignored it like I usually do,
but this time for some reason I just knew that this was going to be a bad storm.
This window we're getting ready to go through is how I had escaped from the home
after escape coming out of the bathroom where I took shelter.
You had someone with you, right?
My sister and my three dogs were the only people here.
My husband is still in Michigan.
This is how I normally would go out through the house.
There was a two by four that was blocking here or actually of this big board that fell down.
Water started coming if you look inside the bathroom, water started coming down through the ceiling.
What did you use in here to take cover?
We had two pillows, a very large quilt.
We got in the bathtub.
All of us, well, myself, my sister and my three dogs got in the bathtub and that's where we took cover.
This is the master.
As you can see, there is debris everywhere.
Mud, leaves, trees, you name it.
There wasn't much to salvage in here at all.
My sheets were out of my bed, clearly made, is all in here.
Yeah, pillows inside the shower.
They obviously don't belong there.
But we tried to get as much as we could out of here and take it to a storage unit to try and dry out.
Whether it makes it or not, I couldn't tell you.
The table that you're seeing and that red piece were actually inside the dining room are the breakfast knook, what they call it.
All my living room furniture, everything is now in the foyer for the most part.
Yeah, I mean, it's just, it's pulled everything out. I can't believe this.
And be careful.
I really smell full of food.
We found somehow this ended up inside the dishwasher.
We didn't know what it was to.
It was actually a glass shelf.
My husband had put up for me inside the dishwasher.
So what do you think saved your life?
Being prepared, I guess, you know, taking heed when I had heard that the weather was going to be really bad.
And my trusty little weather radio, I mean, $35 from Walmart, it told me what I need to know, where it was headed,
and what was going on.
We had lost power, I guess, earlier in the morning.
We had no satellite or anything.
So just like Sootylery said, being prepared is what saved her life.
Have an action plan and know where you're going to go.
Have your weather radio, flashlights, and everything you need to survive.
And also make sure your emergency information is up today in AMC's Emergency Notification System
and the Army's Disaster Personnel and Accountability System.
Thank you for tuning in, and be sure to check us out online at www.amc.army.mil.
I'm Cherish Washington reporting from Redstone Arsenal.
